title: The road to Pandharpur
hookLine: a wet road out of Alandi, white caps and saffron flags, cymbals that don't stop for the rain: the Varkaris are walking to Pandharpur
carry: the wari: the walking and singing are the worship
tomorrow: why does Vitthal stand on a brick, hands on hips?
last: THE LORD SITS IN EVERY HEART, WHATEVER THE CASTE.

lines: A WET ROAD OUT OF ALANDI.
cards: The road out of Alandi is wet, and it's moving. Men in white, small saffron flags over their shoulders. Women with tulsi plants in brass pots balanced on their heads.

Cymbals keeping a beat that doesn't stop for the rain. Nobody here is in a hurry, and nobody is standing still. They're walking toward Pandharpur, a temple town in Maharashtra, to stand before the god they call Vitthal.
This is Maharashtra's Varkari tradition, and this week i walk with it.

teach.b: Varkaris call the pilgrimage the wari, and a Varkari is someone who keeps it, who goes again and again. So it isn't a visit. It's a walk, kept up across a life.
The arriving matters, but so does every step, and the songs sung on the road are part of the worship, not something to pass the time.

Year three gave you the saints of this road as stories: Jnaneshwar, the outcast boy who opened the Gita in Marathi; Namdev, whose bowl of milk Vitthal drank; Tukaram, whose sunk notebooks came back up from the river.
To Varkaris, those saints aren't only people in old books.
They went first, and they're still on the road. The walkers don't go as scattered strangers, either.
They go in dindis, singing groups, each with its own flag and its own leader keeping the song going.

Someone who sets out alone is folded into a dindi and its music: you eat with them, sleep near them, and sing their verses until they're yours. And there's no single gate you pass to become a Varkari, no exam.
Tradition speaks of the name of Vitthal on the lips, a necklace of tulsi beads at the throat, and the road under the feet. The temple is at the end.
But for the length of the wari, the road itself is where the god is sung.
That's bhakti, devotion, as a habit of the feet: you keep coming back, singing with your group, and the coming back is the worship.

how: Varkaris walk to Pandharpur in singing groups called dindis, carrying flags and tulsi, singing the abhangs of their saints along the way.

games.why: the wari is walked together: a lone walker is folded into a dindi and sings its verses until they're theirs.

practice: Press both feet gently into the floor and feel the weight of you carried down into the ground. Then walk, in your mind, one road you've walked many times, to school, to work, to a parent's door, one step for each breath.
If you pray, you can carry a name you use for God along that road, the way the Varkaris carry Vitthal's.
